original_question: Determine how adding birth and death processes changes the dynamics, existence theory, and spatially non-constant steady-state profiles of the dynamic-memory movement models introduced in Section 2.2.2.
target_in_paper: Open Problem 13 in Section 2.2.2 (Dynamic memory): how the movement-only dynamic-memory models discussed there change when birth/death processes are added.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the right section of the paper (Sect. 2.2.2), the correct modification (adding birth/death processes), and the same three substantive targets asked in the paper's official formulation: changes in dynamics, existence of solutions, and changes in spatially non-constant steady-state solutions.
missing_details: The nearest official target is specifically Open Problem 13, not a broader question about all cognition-based PDEs in the paper.

The surrounding context narrows the intended scope to the movement-only dynamic-memory models presented up to that point in Sect. 2.2.2, before the paper turns to consumer-resource systems that already include population dynamics.
The paper explicitly separates existence for the time-dependent problem from existence for the steady-state problem; your draft compresses these into the broader phrase 'existence theory.'

To be stand-alone, the model class should be identified as nonlocal advection-diffusion PDEs for population densities u_i(x,t), with dynamic cognitive-map quantities such as p_i(x,t) or k_i(x,t), and with perception given by the spatial convolution a_{g,R}(x,t)=∫_Ω a(y,t)g(x-y)dy.

The nearby context makes the motivation a timescale issue: omitting birth/death may be reasonable only when movement is much faster than demographic change, but this can conflict with quasi-steady-state reductions for dynamic cognitive-map equations.

Open Problem 13 does not fix a particular demographic term, boundary condition, domain, or kernel choice, so a paper-faithful rewrite should preserve that generality rather than inserting a specific logistic, linear, or other birth/death law.
The official wording asks how solution profiles change for spatially non-constant steady-state solutions; this is slightly narrower than an unrestricted classification of all steady states.

Ambient ring/field, homogeneity, degree restrictions, nilpotency conditions, and phrases like 'for all sufficiently large m' are not part of this PDE open problem; the relevant hidden details are instead the variables, operators, scope of the model class, and the time-dependent versus steady-state quantifiers.
refined_question: For the movement-only dynamic-memory models from Sect. 2.2.2 of Wang and Salmaniw—namely nonlocal advection-diffusion population models in which the density u_i(x,t) is biased by a dynamic cognitive map, possibly through auxiliary map variables such as p_i(x,t) or k_i(x,t), with perception operator a_{g,R}(x,t)=∫_Ω a(y,t)g(x-y)dy—how does augmenting the population equation(s) by birth/death processes change the qualitative dynamics? In particular, do the resulting time-dependent and steady-state problems admit solutions, and how are the existence and profiles of spatially non-constant steady states altered relative to the corresponding movement-only models?
justification: This is the paper's Open Problem 13 almost verbatim. The draft already tracks the official problem closely, but the paper's nearby context shows that the intended scope is the movement-only dynamic-memory systems introduced in Sect. 2.2.2, not a broader class of cognitive PDEs. The same context also explains why birth/death is being added at all: the authors warn that separating movement and demographic timescales can make quasi-steady-state simplifications questionable, so they ask for a re-analysis of dynamics, solvability of both the time-dependent and steady-state problems, and the effect on spatially non-constant steady-state profiles after demographic terms are introduced. The paper does not state an equivalent reformulation of this open problem.
